extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, newspaper editors, and students of newspaper production
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and professional guidance on producing newspapers and training newspapermen, covering technology, economics, editorial policy, staffing, and the education required of journalists. Draws on late-19th-century industry changes (presses, typesetting, paper, news agencies) to recommend production and editorial practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of news associations (United Press) to supply world news
rubrics_metrics.description: “The system which is most perfectly organized is the establishment known as the United Press. It supplies the news of the whole world, so that the individual editor sitting at his desk has only to look after the news of his own locality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join or rely on wire agencies/associations so the paper receives comprehensive national and international news; this obviates much of the drudgery of news-getting and lets the editor focus on local news and intellectual work. Economies of scale divide the large expense among many papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt modern printing machinery (large presses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern presses can turn out large sheets and deliver twenty thousand finished papers in an hour; machines fold, count, and prepare piles so dealers need not count them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in up-to-date presses to enable large editions, faster production, accurate counting and folding. This revolutionizes production and distribution logistics compared with hand-press methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical typesetters (Mergenthaler / Linotype)
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine operated with keys like a piano can set type by mechanical means (e.g., the Mergenthaler/Linotype), forming lines, casting slugs, and producing pages ready for press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt mechanical typesetting to cut typesetting costs substantially (reported as about half the cost of hand-setting), while being aware of trade-offs: machine-set pages may be less typographically handsome than hand-set pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make stereotype plates and use photographic/zinc plate reproduction for illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages are printed from stereotype plates (whole-page plates with curve to fit the press). Photographs can be transferred to a prepared zinc plate and etched with acid so the picture is ready for printing without wood engraving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stereotype plates for efficient printing and modern photo-engraving techniques for illustrations to reduce time and expense of reproducing portraits and pictures versus traditional wood engraving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage paper sourcing and costs (shift to wood pulp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper manufacture moved from rags to rye straw to wood; modern newspaper paper is made of wood pulp (spruce/pine), causing a steep decline in cost — historically from 12–20 cents to about 2¼ cents a pound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand raw-material sources and their effects on cost and production quality. Lower paper costs make large cheap editions feasible and materially affect profitability and pricing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate capital, plant, and utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A large newspaper establishment requires substantial capital — not less than about a million dollars — including multiple big presses (costly), electric lighting, dynamos, steam engines, and suitable quarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for significant upfront investment in presses, electrical plant, and facilities; factor in rent or building ownership and equipment costs when evaluating feasibility of starting or maintaining a big paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the kind of newspaper and target readership
rubrics_metrics.description: “What kind of a newspaper will you make? ... will you make a newspaper for sensible people? or will you make a newspaper for fools?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide editorially whether the paper targets an intelligent/educated readership or a mass/popular audience. Both are legitimate commercial choices; choose based on market, principles, and the sort of journalism you wish to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on Sunday editions and consider moral/social implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists about the propriety of Sunday newspapers; however, public demand drives their production and large Sunday editions can be very profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh public demand and commercial advantages of Sunday editions against personal or community conscience objections; if there is market demand, many papers will publish Sundays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial independence and faithfulness to principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper is naturally an organ of a party, but the paper and editor should not blindly follow party when the party is wrong; 'The newspaper must be independent of its party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should know and clearly express their principles, be willing to break with their party when warranted, and preserve the paper's integrity and public trust rather than mere party loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and knowledge requirements for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: The young journalist should learn everything possible; a strict, classical education (Greek, Latin) and especially mastery of the English language are prized. He should also know practical sciences (chemistry, electricity), history, American Constitution and constitutional law; political economy requires attention though is 'dismal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train journalists broadly: deep language skills, classical grounding where possible, and familiarity with relevant sciences and law. Mastery of English is critical to avoid saying what one does not mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize news acquisition but use associations to reduce labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically it was vital to 'look out for the news' and not be beaten; however, procuring the news is increasingly provided for by associations in which newspapers combine to supply news of the city, country, and world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep competitive on scoops and timely reporting, but leverage cooperative arrangements for routine local and national returns (e.g., election returns) so resources can be shifted to deeper study and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire better educated and more capable staff; include women reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanization has led to fewer employees but they tend to be better educated and more capable. Many newspapers employ ladies as reporters, writers, and artists, though retention can be an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in recruiting and paying competent, educated staff (including women); recognize market pressures on retention and plan for turnover while valuing the contributions of female journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrations and photographs to enhance appeal and reduce costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers now abound in pictures; photographic processes to zinc plates mean portraits that once cost $30–$50 can now cost about $1.25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit modern photographic and photo-engraving methods to include portraits and illustrations affordably, increasing reader interest and newspaper attractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electric lighting and modern utilities for working conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric lighting is indispensable for newspaper offices; gas lighting caused excessive heat and fainting among workers in summer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement electric lighting (driven by dynamos using press steam engines) to improve working conditions, reduce heat-related problems and enable comfortable night work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance cost-saving mechanization with quality concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanization (typesetting, presses) cheapens production, but there are aesthetic/quality trade-offs (e.g., Linotype pages may not be as handsome as hand-set pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt machines to reduce costs and increase throughput but monitor typographical and editorial quality; make conscious trade-offs between economy and craftsmanship.
